slides.title: One robot, independent moving agents
slides.message: The controlled robot must reach its goal without access to the true future of other agents.
slides.script: This simulation illustrates the task: one controlled robot and independent moving agents. The agents did not coordinate their avoidance with my robot. My rover had to reach a goal while avoiding fixed obstacles, moving agents, and the arena boundary. It could use their current observed positions, but not their true future motion. I evaluated both arrival and clearance, because staying still can look safe while completely failing the task.
slides.transition: To evaluate that behavior, I first need to define success.

slides.title: Defining success
slides.message: Success means reaching the goal safely.
points: **Clearance:** center distance minus both safety radii
**Safe:** no collision, no arena exit, no execution error
**Goal:** final position within the chosen tolerance
slides.script: To evaluate the robot, I first defined what success means. I model the robot and each obstacle or agent as circles. Clearance is the distance between their centers, minus both radii. Positive clearance means the circles are separated. Zero means they touch; negative clearance means the modeled envelopes overlap. Then I use three binary indicators. I safe is one when there is no collision, no arena exit, and no execution error. I goal is one when the robot finishes within the goal tolerance. I joint is their product. So a successful run must be safe and reach the goal.
slides.transition: With those criteria defined, I can explain the system's assumptions and limits.
slides.hook: Safety alone is not enough: a robot that never moves can still fail the task.

slides.title: What the system had to handle
slides.message: The planner, online state and physical drivetrain have different kinds of limits.
slides.script: I had local agent observations, a bounded arena, and a robot that couldn't move sideways. The offline plan used soft speed and acceleration penalties. Online, I clipped internal acceleration and velocity. These mechanisms are different, and they don't prove universal bounds on physical motion.
slides.transition: I organized the system into an offline plan and an online correction.

slides.title: The two-layer architecture
slides.message: The nominal plan handles the known static scene; current observations drive the local correction.
slides.script: The first layer builds a nominal trajectory using the static scene: the start, goal, fixed obstacles, and arena. Moving agents are excluded. The second layer runs during execution. It combines attraction toward the nominal path with repulsion from current observations and damping. I then convert that planar request into wheel commands. The overhead camera closes the loop, and the logs let me inspect positions, forces, commands, and timing afterward. This separation kept the global path problem away from the real-time loop.
slides.transition: Before looking inside each layer, here is what I contributed.

slides.title: What I optimized
slides.message: I optimized interior trajectory points with a discrete cost and fixed endpoints.
slides.script: I discretized the path into points over a fixed horizon. The first and last points stayed fixed, so the optimizer changed only the interior coordinates. The cost combines a kinetic term, the static-scene potential, a smoothing term, and penalties for speed and acceleration violations. The potential attracts toward the goal and discourages obstacles and walls. One important detail is the difference between a penalty and a hard constraint. A high cost discourages a violation; it doesn't make that violation impossible. I supplied an analytical gradient to the local optimizer and checked it against finite differences.
slides.transition: The starting path also matters, because the optimization is local.

details.label: Variables
details.question: What exactly is the decision vector?
details.answer: It contains x and y for each interior point: 2(N−1) scalar coordinates, with the endpoints reconstructed unchanged.
reason: N intervals create N+1 points.

slides.title: Making the offline problem usable
slides.message: I replaced the earlier inverse-distance potential with a smooth compact potential.
slides.script: The earlier inverse-distance potential created difficult numerical behavior near obstacles. I moved to a compact polynomial potential. With exponent three, its value, slope and curvature go to zero at the cutoff, giving the optimizer a smoother objective. I kept a finite obstacle-core treatment and checked the gradient and route diagnostics. This formulation change is documented, but I don't have an isolated convergence benchmark. I explain the numerical reason without claiming a measured speedup.
slides.transition: Once the nominal route was available, I had to react during execution.

details.label: Earlier formulation
details.question: What was wrong with inverse distance?
details.answer: Near-zero distance can create extreme gradients; a cutoff can also create poor smoothness if handled badly.
reason: The draft documents the replacement.
The exact quantitative effect was not isolated in a paired benchmark.

Near contact: rapidly increasing value and gradient

details.return_line: The formulation became smoother, with no isolated speedup claimed.

details.label: Evidence
details.question: What evidence supports the change?
details.answer: The code retains both inverse-distance and compact-polynomial functions, and the draft explains why the smoother version was introduced.
reason: This supports the implementation decision.
It does not supply a measured before/after runtime gain.

compact_base = max(0.0, 1.0 - normalized_distance**2)
return compact_base**power
visual.caption: Exact compact-kernel excerpt · cost.py

details.label: Smooth cutoff
details.question: Why exponent three?
details.answer: At d=R, the compact cubic in 1−(d/R)² has zero value, first derivative and second derivative.
reason: That gives C² continuity at the support boundary.

details.return_line: The formulation became smoother, with no isolated speedup claimed.

slides.title: What the online corrector sees
slides.message: Each update starts from measured robot state and current obstacle snapshots.
points: **Reference:** a point ahead on the nominal
slides.script: Each update starts from the robot position and heading measured by the camera. Velocity is estimated and filtered from observations. Moving obstacles arrive as current snapshots with freshness information. The corrector also gets a point ahead on the nominal. On hardware, this reference follows measured path progress, so it doesn't simply run away in time while the robot falls behind. No agent future is needed.

slides.title: How the correction is built
slides.message: Attraction, three repulsions and damping combine before acceleration clipping.
slides.script: The correction has five contributions. Attraction pulls toward the look-ahead reference. Moving-agent repulsion reacts to the currently observed disturbance. Fixed-obstacle and boundary terms add local protection around the planned route. Damping opposes the estimated velocity. I sum these terms, divide by the model mass, and clip the acceleration. The repulsion uses edge-to-edge clearance, with a small numerical floor, and falls to zero at its influence limit. This is a soft force model. Strong repulsion can dominate attraction or keep the response saturated, so the force plot is useful for understanding poor progress. It is not a formal collision-avoidance proof.
slides.transition: I'll show the order of operations for one update.

details.label: Attraction
details.question: What pulls the robot back toward the route?
details.answer: A proportional force points from the measured position to the nominal look-ahead reference.
reason: A larger gain increases the request, not necessarily physical speed.
Clipping and wheel conversion follow.

k_a = 5.0 in the reported physical profile

details.label: Agent repulsion

details.answer: It points away from the agent and increases as the modeled clearance decreases.

slides.title: One control step
slides.message: The physical experiment uses semi-implicit Euler, followed by real wheel-command conversion.
slides.script: The experimental corrector uses semi-implicit Euler. I compute the force from the current observation, divide by the model mass, and limit the acceleration norm. Then I update and limit the velocity. The position update uses that new velocity, which is the semi-implicit part. On hardware, that position is a one-step intention; I don't replace the next camera measurement with it. The physical controller reconciles its internal velocity with observed motion, then converts the request into heading and wheel commands. Velocity-Verlet and stiff repulsion are comparison variants in the study. I don't present them as three controllers deployed on the bench.
slides.transition: The next distinction is what information this update is allowed to use.

reason: Measured state anchors every physical update.

details.label: Integration scheme
details.question: Why call it semi-implicit Euler?

slides.title: Causal does not mean blind
slides.message: Looking ahead on my stored plan is different from knowing an agent’s true future.
slides.script: Causal means the controller doesn't read an agent's true future position. Looking ahead on its own stored path is allowed: that plan is already known. The physical interface receives current obstacle snapshots. Prediction from past observations could also be causal, but it is different from reading a scenario's future. I keep that information boundary explicit.
slides.transition: Even with that information boundary, a local controller can still fail.

details.label: Interfaces
details.question: How does the interface enforce the boundary?
details.answer: The offline builder excludes agents, and the physical corrector accepts ObservedMobileObstacle snapshots.

slides.title: A safe run could still stall
slides.message: An early physical adapter timed out with weak translation; later work addressed the force-to-motion chain.
slides.script: An early physical trial had active repulsion and no collision, but translation stayed weak and the run timed out. A nonzero force wasn't enough. I inspected how that force became motion and wheel commands. The later chain used force over mass, velocity integration, a progress-based reference and a characterized drivetrain. Several settings evolved, so I don't attribute later success to one isolated fix.

slides.title: Building the physical testbed
slides.message: I integrated external vision, onboard computation and serial actuation into one measured loop.
slides.script: The overhead Basler camera observes the marked arena. Its stream reaches the rover's Raspberry Pi through an access point and Wi-Fi. The Pi runs vision and control, then sends wheel commands over onboard serial. This made the full chain visible and measurable.

slides.title: From a planar command to wheel motion
slides.message: I implemented heading and wheel conversion above the supplier’s motor execution.
slides.script: A planar velocity isn't a wheel command. I turn its direction into a desired heading and compare it with the measured forward direction. The controller chooses driving or pivoting, then combines translation and rotation into left and right commands. It rescales, limits and smooths the pair. Reverse is available with switching thresholds. I implemented this high-level conversion; supplier firmware executes the motor inputs. With no wheel encoders, feedback came from the camera.
slides.transition: That made position accuracy a central part of the control problem.

details.label: Heading conversion
details.question: How do you get heading from velocity?
details.answer: The desired heading is atan2(v_y,v_x); the error is wrapped relative to measured robot-forward yaw.
reason: The marker-to-forward axis offset is calibrated.
Yaw-rate feed-forward and heading feedback form the turn request.

visual.text:
φ = atan2(v_y, v_x)
e_ψ = wrap(φ − ψ_robot)
ω_req = sat(κ_ff φ̇; k_ω) + 2 k_θ k_ω e_ψ
visual.caption: Physical conversion / draft Eq. (25)–(26)

details.return_line: My high-level conversion sits above the supplier's motor execution.

details.label: Wheel mapping
details.question: How are wheel commands formed?
details.answer: The nominal pair is linear minus angular on the left, and linear plus angular on the right, followed by joint rescaling, floors and smoothing.
reason: Rescaling preserves the pair ratio before later floors.
Command units are normalized driver inputs, not measured wheel velocities.

visual.text:
u_L = u_v − u_ω
u_R = u_v + u_ω
Then: joint limit → effective floor → smoothing
visual.caption: Draft Eq. (28), physical implementation

details.return_line: My high-level conversion sits above the supplier's motor execution.

details.label: Reverse motion
details.question: What does reverse change?
details.answer: When the heading error crosses an entry threshold, the controller reverses the drive sign and reflects the desired heading by π.
reason: It exits at a separate threshold and clears smoothing history.
Both final blocks use about 92° thresholds; no disabled-reverse ablation isolates its benefit.
details.return_line: My high-level conversion sits above the supplier's motor execution.

details.label: Provided firmware
details.question: Was the low-level control a black box?
details.answer: The supplier source is available. It contains multiple motor paths; the no-encoder rover uses external camera feedback rather than wheel-level feedback in this experiment.
reason: setGoalSpeed has a PID branch for mainType==3 and an open-loop branch otherwise.
I did not write or retune that supplier firmware; the flashed build digest is missing.

visual.caption: Shortened supplier excerpt · setGoalSpeed

details.return_line: My high-level conversion sits above the supplier's motor execution.

slides.title: Diagnosing position error
slides.message: Lens distortion and raised-marker parallax produced two different measured errors.
slides.script: I found two position-error problems. First, lens distortion remained after homography. I calibrated the intrinsics and recomputed the mapping. Across nine ground positions, mean error fell from 36.3 to 5.8 millimeters. Second, the raised rover marker caused parallax because it was above the ground plane. After height correction, mean error fell from 60.8 to 11.6 millimeters across five rover positions. These are separate measurements. The residual error still matters when interpreting small clearances.
slides.transition: Position accuracy was one part of the problem. I also had to keep the loop fast enough.

details.label: Intrinsics
details.question: What did intrinsic calibration change?
details.answer: It estimated camera parameters and lens distortion from twenty valid calibration-board views before metric mapping.
reason: The reported reprojection RMS is 0.191 pixels.
That pixel residual is not the metric rover-position error.
details.return_line: The ground error and raised-marker error remain separate measurements.

details.label: Homography
details.question: Why recompute the homography?
details.answer: The homography must map the distortion-corrected image coordinates to the ground plane.
reason: Four ground markers establish the metric reference.
A plane mapping cannot by itself remove height parallax.

visual.text:
x̃_metric = H x̃_undistorted
x_metric = [x̃₁/x̃₃, x̃₂/x̃₃]ᵀ
visual.caption: Planar mapping / draft Eq. (5)

details.return_line: The ground error and raised-marker error remain separate measurements.

details.label: Parallax geometry
details.question: How did marker height cause error?
details.answer: A raised marker projects along a camera ray to the wrong point on the ground mapping. I applied radial height correction about the principal point.
reason: The draft assumes an approximately normal optical axis.
The controlled marker height is 0.1585 m; camera height is 2.07 m.
details.return_line: The ground error and raised-marker error remain separate measurements.

details.label: Measurement protocol
details.question: Are the two percentage reductions comparable?
details.answer: They are separate within-protocol improvements, not two estimates of the same final accuracy.
reason: Ground: nine known positions, intrinsics plus recomputed homography.
Raised: five positions, before and after parallax correction.
details.return_line: The ground error and raised-marker error remain separate measurements.

slides.hook: Calibration and marker height caused two different errors.

slides.title: Finding the real-time bottleneck
slides.message: Vision dominated the measured loop budget; the correction itself was small.
slides.script: I profiled the whole loop. In the single-agent block, vision averaged about 33 milliseconds, including 29 for detection. Serial took about 8.4 milliseconds; correction took 0.72. Perception was the bottleneck. I tried downscaling before detection. The sessions showed faster processing, but scenarios and agent behavior also differed, so this wasn't an isolated causal test. And a near-20 Hz rate does not establish 50-millisecond sensor-to-action latency.
slides.transition: Once the full chain was running, I tested how repeatable the behavior was.

slides.title: Results, limits, and what I learned
slides.message: The strongest evidence is the complete measured chain; the tested domain remains narrow.
slides.script: This work taught me to test the whole chain. I improved localization, profiled timing, and measured repeated physical behavior. Simulation didn't directly describe the robot: heading constraints, actuation and delay changed the motion. Forty successful outcomes don't erase earlier stalls or marker-loss stops; they describe the selected tasks and settings. The transferable process is to inspect a failure, change a specific part, and measure again with a clear protocol.
